name: Cricket Bowling Variations
description: Checks if models can correctly name different types of cricket deliveries and bowling variations from descriptions.
system_prompt: You are a cricket bowling variation naming assistant. You are given a short description of a cricket delivery, and you must reply with the standard name used by most modern cricketers and commentators. If there are multiple common names, reply with the most common one or a short list of the most common options. Keep answers concise and to the point, and do not include names of other deliveries that are not being described.

tests.prompt: Fast bowler. Very full ball that lands right at the batter's feet, almost on the popping crease, aimed at the base of middle and leg stump.
Fast bowler. Full ball that does not pitch and reaches the batter above the waist on the full.
Fast bowler from over the wicket to a right-hander. Short-pitched delivery that climbs steeply towards the batter's head or chest, forcing them to duck or play a defensive shot.
Right-arm fast bowler, over the wicket to a right-hander. The ball starts outside off stump and swings further away, drawing the batter into a drive and taking the edge.
Right-arm fast bowler, over the wicket to a right-hander. The ball starts on a fourth-stump line and swings late into the pads and stumps.
Right-arm fast bowler with an older ball. To a right-hander, the ball starts wide outside off stump and then swings late in the opposite direction to conventional swing, back into the batter.
Right-arm fast bowler with an older ball. To a right-hander, the ball is angled in towards leg stump and then swings late away from the batter towards the slips, opposite to conventional inswing.
Fast bowler bowls a slower ball by releasing it from the back of the hand with the seam scrambled, causing it to dip and arrive later than expected.
answers: back of the hand slower ball

tests.prompt: Fast bowler delivers a slower ball by digging fingers into the seam so that it comes out of the front of the hand but rolls off the fingers like an off-break.
Fast bowler delivers a slower ball that moves away off the pitch like a leg-spinner, rolling off the fingers towards the leg side for a right-hander.
Fast bowler. Slower ball where the ball is held on the fingertips and released with minimal backspin so it floats and dips, often used at the death.
Right-arm leg-spinner to a right-handed batter. The ball pitches outside leg stump and turns sharply across the batter towards off stump, away from the bat.

Right-arm leg-spinner to a right-handed batter. The bowler uses a disguised wrist position so that the ball appears like a normal leg break, but after pitching it turns into the right-hander from off to leg.
Right-arm leg-spinner. The ball is delivered with more overspin, causing it to dip and bounce more, going straight on or only turning slightly after pitching.
Right-arm leg-spinner. The ball is squeezed out from under the fingers with backspin so that it skids low after pitching, often trapping the batter lbw.
Right-arm off-spinner to a right-handed batter. The ball pitches just outside off stump and turns back into the batter towards middle and leg.

Right-arm off-spinner to a right-handed batter. The bowler uses a different wrist and finger action so that the ball looks like a normal off break, but after pitching it turns away from the batter like a leg-break.
Right-arm spinner flicks the ball with the middle finger off the front of the hand, producing extra skid and a small amount of turn, often from around the wicket to a right-hander.
Left-arm orthodox spinner to a right-handed batter. The ball pitches outside off stump and turns back into the pads from off to leg.
Left-arm wrist-spinner (chinaman) to a right-handed batter. The ball pitches outside off stump and turns sharply into the batter from off to leg, like a right-arm leg break from the other side.
